title: Telling wine cultivars apart from their chemistry
text:
Description: “Classifying Italian wines by cultivar with logistic regression.”
Data: Wine recognition dataset, bundled with scikit-learn. Original source: Aeberhard, S. and Forina, M. (1992). Wine [Dataset]. UCI Machine Learning Repository. https://doi.org/10.24432/C5PC7J. Licensed CC BY 4.0.
The dataset has 13 chemical measurements for 178 wines grown in the same region of Italy by three different cultivars. The question: how well does chemistry alone identify the cultivar, and do a couple of measurements do most of the work?

title: Telling wine cultivars apart from their chemistry
text:
Setup

import sys
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

This confirms the post rendered with the project’s own Python environment. The path should end in .venv, then Scripts or bin, then the Python executable.

print(Path(sys.executable).parts[-3:])

('.venv', 'Scripts', 'python.exe')

wine = load_wine(as_frame=True)
df = wine.frame.copy()
df["cultivar"] = df["target"].map(dict(enumerate(wine.target_names)))

Figure 1 plots two of those measurements against each other. The three cultivars form mostly separate clusters, with some overlap between class_0 and class_1.

title: Telling wine cultivars apart from their chemistry
text:
Classifying cultivars
I fit a standardised logistic regression and score it with 5-fold cross-validation, first on all 13 features and then on only the two from Figure 1.

X_all = df[wine.feature_names]
X_two = df[["color_intensity", "flavanoids"]]
y = df["target"]

model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
scores_all = cross_val_score(model, X_all, y, cv=5)
scores_two = cross_val_score(model, X_two, y, cv=5)

results = pd.DataFrame({
    "features": ["all 13", "colour intensity + flavanoids"],
    "mean_accuracy": [scores_all.mean(), scores_two.mean()],
    "sd": [scores_all.std(), scores_two.std()],
}).round(3)

title: Telling wine cultivars apart from their chemistry
text:
What I found
With all 13 features the model reaches a mean cross-validated accuracy of 98.3%. Using only colour intensity and flavanoids it still reaches 88.8%. Two measurements carry most of the signal, and the remaining eleven mainly resolve the class_0 and class_1 overlap visible in the scatter plot.

title: Fifty-five years of life expectancy
text:
Description: “How life expectancy changed by continent from 1952 to 2007, and how it tracks income.
Data: gapminder R package by Jennifer Bryan, an excerpt of data from Gapminder. The package is released under CC0 and the underlying Gapminder data under CC BY 4.0.
The data covers 142 countries every five years from 1952 to 2007. Two questions: which continents gained the most life expectancy over that period, and how closely does life expectancy track income?

title: Fifty-five years of life expectancy
text:
Setup

library(gapminder)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

title: Fifty-five years of life expectancy
text:
A first look

gapminder |>
  summarise(
    countries = n_distinct(country),
    continents = n_distinct(continent),
    first_year = min(year),
    last_year = max(year)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  countries continents first_year last_year
      <int>      <int>      <int>     <int>
1       142          5       1952      2007

title: Fifty-five years of life expectancy
text:
Gains by continent

change <- gapminder |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  summarise(
    life_1952 = median(lifeExp[year == 1952]),
    life_2007 = median(lifeExp[year == 2007]),
    gain = life_2007 - life_1952
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(gain))

kable(change, digits = 1)

title: Fifty-five years of life expectancy
text:
Life expectancy and income in 2007

gap_2007 <- filter(gapminder, year == 2007)

ggplot(gap_2007, aes(gdpPercap, lifeExp, colour = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  scale_size_area(guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "GDP per capita (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)", colour = "Continent") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Life expectancy against GDP per capita in 2007. Point size is population. The x axis is on a log scale.






fit <- lm(lifeExp ~ log10(gdpPercap), data = gap_2007)
coef(fit)

     (Intercept) log10(gdpPercap) 
        4.949612        16.585064 

summary(fit)$r.squared

[1] 0.654449

title: Fifty-five years of life expectancy
text:
What I found
On a log scale the relationship in Figure 1 is close to linear. The model says each tenfold increase in GDP per capita goes with about 16.6 more years of life expectancy, and income alone explains 65% of the variation across countries in 2007. The points furthest below the line are mostly African countries, which matches Africa having the lowest median life expectancy in both 1952 and 2007 (Table 1).

title: ArunarkSingh
text:
I completed my Bachelor’s of Applied Science in Electrical Engineering from UBC, and I also specialize in the field of Machine Learning. Because of my interest in ML and Data Science, i decided to further persue MDS at UBC, helping me deepen my knowledge and apply the knowledge in the real world.
As a kid I was always curious about the technology that surrounded me, always exploring and always learning. This curiosity is what led me towards electrical engineering at UBC for my bachelors, and what led me to research and dig deep into Machine Learning and Deep Learning systems. I did a bunch of projects, performed research with professors, just to deepen my knowledge of Machine Learning systems. And this is why I am pursuing Master’s of Data Science at UBC, I want to understand and use the Data and information around us to build systems that actually make decisions better, not just process numbers. MDS is giving me the statistical and engineering foundation to go from research-scale ML to something that can work reliably in the real world, and that’s the direction I want to take my career.

title: About
text:
I grew up with strong ties to both Oman and India, and moved to Vancouver for my undergrad. I completed my Bachelor of Applied Science in Electrical and Computer Engineering at UBC, where I spent most of my time in research: working on protein language models in a computational biology lab, and later on vision transformer and diffusion architectures. Alongside that, I taught robotics and coding part-time to elementary school students, which turned out to be one of the more grounding parts of my week.
And I have done so many, and I mean so many ML related projects for fun and to gain the depth.

title: About

Why data science
My path into data science came through research, not a classroom. Working with large models and large datasets, I kept running into the same bottleneck: the hard part usually wasn’t the model, it was the data. MDS is where I’m building the statistical and engineering foundation I was missing, so I can move between research-style ML and the kind of data work that actually ships.

Outside of data science
Outside of work, I play soccer and basketball, and I’m slowly getting better at neither. I keep a small garden going, mostly tulsi, and chilli, alongside some Pothos and Peperomia that are much harder to kill than the vegetables. I read manga, play games on the PS4 when I get the time, and I build small interactive web projects for fun, usually something no one asked for but that I wanted to see exist.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Orientation week was a bit of a whiplash after four years of undergrad. I came in from an Electrical and Computer Engineering background, having spent most of my final year buried in machine learning research rather than classes, so sitting in a room full of new classmates from economics, biology, and computer science backgrounds was a good reminder of how differently people think about the same data problems. The first few days were less about content and more about tooling: getting comfortable with the terminal, setting up Git and GitHub properly, and realizing how much of this program runs on version control and reproducibility rather than one-off scripts.
The first week of actual classes moved fast. What surprised me most was how much emphasis is placed on communication and workflow, things like commit hygiene, writing for a reader who isn’t you, and publishing work publicly, rather than just the statistics and modeling I expected to be the focus. Coming from a research background where a lot of code lived in a single Colab notebook, having to think about project structure, .gitignore-style discipline, and a live website from week one has been a useful shift.
A few weeks in, I’m feeling good about the pace. It’s demanding, but in a way that feels productive rather than just busy. I’m looking forward to seeing how the more technical courses build on this foundation, and to having a portfolio that actually reflects the work as I go, instead of scrambling to put one together at the end.

title: R and Python in one post
text:
Description: “Passing data between R and Python with reticulate.”
Data: mtcars, built into R. Henderson, H. V. and Velleman, P. F. (1981), from the 1974 Motor Trend US magazine.
This post passes data from R to Python, fits a line in Python, and passes the fitted coefficients back to R for plotting. It uses the knitr engine, which sends {python} chunks to reticulate in the same session.

title: R and Python in one post
text:
Setup (R)

library(reticulate)
library(ggplot2)

# Chunks run with the working directory set to this post's folder,
# so the project's .venv is two levels up.
use_virtualenv(normalizePath(file.path("..", "..", ".venv")), required = TRUE)

title: R and Python in one post
text:
Prepare the data in R

cars_df <- mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp")]

title: R and Python in one post
text:
Fit the model in Python
r.cars_df reads the R data frame into Python as a pandas DataFrame.

import sys
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np

print(Path(sys.executable).resolve().parts[-3:])

('.venv', 'Scripts', 'python.exe')

cars = r.cars_df
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(cars["wt"], cars["mpg"], 1)
print(f"mpg = {intercept:.2f} - {abs(slope):.2f} * wt")

mpg = 37.29 - 5.34 * wt

title: R and Python in one post
section: Plot in R with the Python result
text:
Plot in R with the Python result
py$slope and py$intercept read the Python values back into R.

ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(intercept = py$intercept, slope = py$slope, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Weight (1000 lbs)", y = "Miles per gallon") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Fuel economy against weight, with the least-squares line fitted in Python.





Each extra 1000 lbs of weight costs about 5.3 miles per gallon.
